This vignette compares the four frequentist regression models in `bayclumpr`. It also shows how to plot a calibration and reconstruct temperatures. If you're new to the package, start with `vignette("bayclumpr", package = "bayclumpr")`.

```{r setup}
library(bayclumpr)
```

## The four models

The models differ in which measurement errors they account for.

| Function | Model | Errors in `Temperature` | Errors in `D47` |
|:---------|:------|:-----------------------:|:---------------:|
| `cal.ols()` | Ordinary least squares | No | No |
| `cal.wols()` | Weighted least squares | No | No |
| `cal.deming()` | Deming regression (`deming` package) | Yes | Yes |
| `cal.york()` | York regression (`IsoplotR` package) | Yes | Yes |

The weights in `cal.wols()` don't come from the reported errors. They come from a regression of the absolute residuals on the fitted values, so observations in regions with more scatter get less weight. `cal.deming()` and `cal.york()` use `TempError` and `D47error` for each observation.

All four functions use bootstrapping. Each replicate resamples the calibration dataset with replacement and fits the model again. The result has one row per replicate, with the intercept (`alpha`), the slope (`beta`), and the residual SD of D47 around the fitted line (`sigma`). The default is 1,000 replicates. Replicates that fail are removed with a warning.

## Fitting the models

We simulate 50 observations under the intermediate error scenario. The true values are `alpha` = 0.268 and `beta` = 0.0369.

```{r}
set.seed(3)
ds <- cal.dataset(error = "S2", nobs = 50)

fits <- list(
  OLS = cal.ols(data = ds),
  WOLS = cal.wols(data = ds),
  Deming = cal.deming(data = ds),
  York = cal.york(data = ds)
)
```

`cal.summary()` gives the estimate, standard error, and 95% interval of each parameter. We combine the summaries of the four models into one table:

```{r}
sums <- lapply(names(fits), function(m) cbind(model = m, cal.summary(fits[[m]])))
do.call(rbind, sums)
```

`SE` is the standard error of each estimate, which is the SD of the bootstrap replicates. `sigma` is itself an SD: the scatter of individual samples around the calibration line.

## Plotting a calibration

`cal.ci()` takes the table of `alpha` and `beta` and returns the median line and its interval over a range of temperatures. Here we plot the York calibration:

```{r}
ci <- cal.ci(fits$York, from = min(ds$Temperature), to = max(ds$Temperature))

plot(D47 ~ Temperature, data = ds, pch = 16, col = "grey50",
     xlab = expression(10^6 / T^2 ~ (K)), ylab = expression(Delta[47]))
polygon(c(ci$x, rev(ci$x)), c(ci$ci_lower_est, rev(ci$ci_upper_est)),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.3), border = NA)
lines(ci$x, ci$median_est, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
```

The `level` argument changes the probability covered by the interval.

## Reconstructing temperatures

`rec.clumped()` reconstructs temperatures from any of these tables. We create a reconstruction dataset with three D47 values, each measured with two levels of precision. Each sample has three replicates (`N`):

```{r}
recData <- data.frame(
  Sample = paste("Sample", 1:6),
  D47 = rep(c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8), 2),
  D47error = rep(c(0.005, 0.02), each = 3),
  N = 3
)

rec.clumped(recData = recData, obCal = fits$York)
```

`meanTemp` is the temperature (°C) from the mean slope and intercept. `SE` is the standard error of the temperature, based on `D47error`. `SD` is the uncertainty of the temperature of a single replicate, based on `D47error` × sqrt(`N`). `median`, `lower`, and `upper` describe the 95% interval, based on `SE`.

By default, both `SD` and `SE` combine the error in `D47` with the spread of slopes and intercepts in the bootstrap. It describes the temperature predicted by the calibration line. With `prediction = TRUE`, it also includes the scatter of individual samples around that line (`sigma`). This is the same kind of uncertainty given by `rec.bayesian()`:

```{r}
rec.clumped(recData = recData, obCal = fits$York, prediction = TRUE)
```

We can also reconstruct the same samples under every model:

```{r}
recs <- lapply(fits, function(f) rec.clumped(recData = recData, obCal = f)$meanTemp)
cbind(recData, do.call(cbind, recs))
```
